title: Anatomy of a Fall, My Cousin Vinny, and the embarrassment of the "courtroom drama"

commenti.body:
>*12 Angry Men* is an unquestioned classic and is quite literally nothing but courtroom processes on screen.

Another example of a 'pure' courtroom drama with canonical status is *Anatomy of a Murder*. There are quite a few other unquestionably canonical movies with courtroom drama elements like *La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc*, *Paths of Glory*, *Breaker Morant*, perhaps *Witness for the Prosecution*, which is another pure courtroom drama.

>I don't understand how it's not enough for a movie to simply be a "good courtroom story" and the expectation that any courtroom plots also feature another offering, like sneaking vegetables into junk food.

I can think of a few other genres with a similar status, like the romantic comedy, the political thriller, the slasher (horror vs. elevated horror), etc. As you said, critics -- and cinephiles in general, to be honest -- have a hard time taking comedies seriously.

“Again, the message I get here is that there's supposedly something embaressing or low-brow about enjoying a good courtroom procedural by itself.”

I’m not really sure you can draw that conclusion from a few review snippets. Any procedural or by the numbers court film, sports film, spy film, etc., isn’t going to be an inventive take on their respective genre. All those reviews are saying is that they believe this film offers more than the baseline of the genre. I don’t think they’re looking down on court films, they would likely say the same about tons of other court films that offer more than the baseline (many of your examples included).

Why would a review specify that Anatomy of a Fall is *just* a courtroom drama? It’s very obviously not just that. The film uses the genre as a tool for exploring the inherent ambiguity of our subjectivity. A courtroom drama is a good tool for this because the task of a trial is the finding of fact, and courtroom dramas (and most movies) typically present a series of events as objective events in the story universe. Anatomy of a fall this turns the genre on its head to make a point about human subjectivity. 

Setting that aside for a moment, films can be exemplars of their respective genre - a great detective story, a great noir, a great thriller, a great comedy, a great horror story, a great court room drama, and so on. But films can do more than just tell good stories using accepted narrative and technical norms. Films can provide the audience with a transcendent experience that forces them to engage in critical reflection about the human experience. This is what great art does. I think Anatomy of a Fall is this kind of movie. It’s not *just* a genre movie. It’s not *just* telling a story. It is a deeply philosophical movie about the limits of our understanding. And it cleverly plays with genre tropes to do this. I think it was really brilliant in a way that most courtroom dramas aren’t.

Slightly off topic, but I read that actual attorneys love My Cousin Vinny because it hews so closely to real life court room procedure. Not just the legal aspect, also things like the competitive but collegial relationship between the attorneys on both sides, the dour judge, etc etc

Courtroom drama is a formula, and these reviews are saying these works go beyond the formula.

I’ve seen most of the John Grisham movies and I could tell you nothing about them. Or the episodes of Suits I’ve seen.

But I can remember 12 Angry Men, even though I saw it 40 years ago. I can remember My Cousin Vinnie, but I haven’t seen it since it came out.

I don’t think it’s deeper than formulaic is bad.

I read a lot of genre fiction, and often think about the difference between genre and formula.

As a trial attorney, it is by far the best movie I’ve ever seen at explaining how attorneys think. Vinny’s cross examination is masterful throughout. Other details that are very accurate are the Judge’s uncompromising attitude towards (perceived or real) disrespect of the formality of the judicial process and the general depiction of the trial itself. It’s also just a phenomenal movie on its own merits
Awesome to hear this confirmed by an actual attorney!
i think four of my law school professors now have said My Cousin Vinny is by far the most accurate movie to a real life courtroom
The most compelling courtroom drama I've seen in years was 2023's Amber Heard vs Johnny Depp defamation trial. The courtroom formula is just too easy.

This is true, and not only that, but My Cousin Vinny is actually often *contrasted* with another film OP mentioned, 12 Angry Men, which is filled with a lot of inaccuracies about the jury deliberation process.

Yes.  Retired atty here.  I have been at “continuing education” seminars for lawyers where speakers show excerpts from the movie to illustrate points about defending a criminal case.  It’s a comedy, yes, but remarkably accurate in terms of courtroom procedure.  And specifically wonderful about how expert testimony properly presented can affect the case.

My perception is that critics who say that “Anatomy of a Fall” is *more* than just a courtroom drama mean that it is more than just a clever “Whodunnit.” 

I too find the movie more compelling than a conventional thriller because it’s not primarily concerned with the question of “did she, or didn’t she, do it?” or even “so what *did* kill Samuel?”    Yet it’s striking to me that some viewers still came out of the film with the complaint that the movie did not answer that first question, and that the ending, for them,  was therefore disappointing.  Certainly,  there are more traditional elements of mystery and suspense in Triet’s evoking the question of “did she do it?” and “will she be acquitted?” Part of the cleverness of the film, though, is the raising of *other* questions, such as “was her son telling the truth?” and even “humanly, if not legally, does she share some blame?”   Also, because its treatment of its subject  is complex and open-ended, it does not resemble the formulaic structure of a half-hour, or hour-long, television drama.  

“Twin Peaks” comes to mind as another example of a genre-subverting treatment of a Whodunnit.   A more traditional courtroom thriller meanwhile — with a definitive resolution via a shock ending — would be 1990’s “Presumed Innocent.”

Cherry on top to me was the prosecution actually realizing ‘you know what, yeah, I think the evidence is pretty weak’. There’s no forced animosity between prosecution and defense. He’s just doing his job with the casual lack of actual interest in the case.

The whole concept is blatantly illegal. You can't introduce new evidence or arguments in the jury room, that's the lawyers' job, and for good reason. It's a good movie, but to someone sufficiently immersed in the theory and practice of real courts, 12 Angry Men can feel like it's depicting a horrific miscarriage of justice, contrary to its intended message

I really don’t understand what you’re getting at…It’s like saying “why can’t Blade Runner just be a compelling sci-fi movie about humans fighting AI? Why does it have to be about identity and memories?” The whole point of courtroom dramas are the themes..12 Angry Men isn’t  loved because it’s a good mystery, it’s because it’s about bias, faulty perception, and the hierarchical elements between the jurors (from what I remember, it’s been like a decade since I’ve seen it). Maybe I’m misinterpreting your argument, but I’m not sure it’s clear haha

I think genre's which tend to adhere somewhat strictly to their form (horror, rom-com, procedurals) are often sorta maligned for being "paint-by-numbers" to a certain degree. 

re: courtroom genre specifically, I think (at least in the US) it might also have something to do with exposure. Law & Order (& similar) have just been a staple of low-effort network television for so long. 


p.s. if youre into the genre, I reallly enjoyed The Caine Mutiny Court Marshall (william friedkin's last pic)!
